title: The clear light
hook: at death, the teachings say, a clear light dawns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bardo, and your line, in between. Did you pause with empty hands between one thing and the next? Yesterday left a light at the end of dying. Today, that light. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

A summer night, and the whole city loses power at once. Streetlights, windows, billboards, gone. For a moment it's just dark, and people stand on their porches, a little uneasy. Then someone looks up and says, oh. Above the rooftops, the sky is full of stars, more than anyone on the block has seen there in years. They hadn't arrived. They'd been there the whole time, drowned out by all the other lights. Tibetan teachers say something like that happens at the end of a life: when every other light goes out, something that was always shining shows itself. Today: the clear light.
screen: `THE CITY GOES DARK.` → `THE STARS WERE ALWAYS THERE.` → `WHEN THE OTHER LIGHTS GO OUT.`

segments.voice: First, what the teachings say. At the end of the bardo of dying, when the senses have withdrawn and the breath has stopped, a clear light dawns. Tibetans call it ösel. The teachers describe it like a clear sky, empty of clouds. It isn't a light from outside, they say. It's the mind's own nature, bare, with nothing covering it. The Bardo Thödol speaks to the person at that moment, by name, and tells them: this is your own mind. Recognize it. Second, the mother and the child. Tibetan teachers use a tender image here. The glimpses of the mind's nature a person meets in meditation during life are called the child clear light. The clear light that dawns at death is called the mother. If the child has been met often enough, they say, then at death the two recognize each other, and meet like a child running into its mother's lap. That's why the practice of a lifetime matters for this moment. Third, an older echo. In a short Pali discourse, the Buddha says the mind is luminous, and that it is stained by defilements that arrive like visitors. Some readers hear in that line the same intuition: underneath the passing stains, something clear. The Tibetan teachings and the Pali text speak in their own ways, and neither needs the other to make its point. Fourth, why this is taught to the living. Teachers say small glimpses come every day: in the gap after a thought, at the edge of sleep, in the moment after a sneeze or a surprise, before the mind starts talking again. The stars over the dark city were never far away. The practice, in this teaching, is learning to notice them before the lights go out.
screen: `ÖSEL: THE MIND'S OWN NATURE, BARE.` · `MOTHER AND CHILD MEET.` · `A LUMINOUS MIND, STAINED BY VISITORS.` · `SMALL GLIMPSES, EVERY DAY.` · then, large: `THE CLEAR LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: sit with open awareness. Close your eyes for three easy breaths, and let the dark be dark. Then open them, slowly, and catch the moment the room appears, before you name a single thing in it. Don't focus anywhere. Let the seeing be wide and plain, like the stars that were there all along. When the naming starts again, close your eyes for a breath and open them once more. Rest in the open seeing for as long as it lasts. The bell holds the time.
The clear light. In Tibetan teaching, the mind's own nature, bare and luminous, which dawns at death and can be glimpsed in life. Today's word.

Your line: the clear light. Today, once, when a light switches on, a lamp, a screen, the sun from behind a cloud, notice the instant of plain seeing before you name what's there. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists prepare for death by practicing recognition of the mind's nature in meditation, the 'child' clear light, so that the 'mother' clear light at death may be recognized; the Bardo Thödol is read aloud to remind the one who has died.

original.note: Sanskrit prabhasvara, luminous; Pali pabhassara, the word for the luminous mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: the light at the end of the tunnel.
what it means: the mind's own nature, bare and luminous, which Tibetan teachings say dawns at death and is glimpsed in meditation.
what a scholar hears: ösel, the meeting of mother and child clear light, and the Pali luminous mind, pabhassara citta, stained by visiting defilements (Anguttara Nikaya 1.51).

notes: AN 1.51 numbering (1.49–52 in some editions) and the paraphrase 'defilements that arrive like visitors' (agantuka): confirm.
The script presents the Pali luminous-mind passage as an echo 'some readers hear', not as the same teaching; Theravada interpreters read it differently. Confirm the framing is fair.
Mother and child clear light: confirm the image and wording.
Daily glimpses (after a thought, edge of sleep, after a sneeze or surprise): attributed to 'teachers'; confirm, especially the sneeze example.
